articles.text: If you are whining that vaccine mandates are un-American and unconstitutional, you are wrong. Being an American citizen gives us incredible rights and freedoms, but it does not give you the right to endanger other people’s lives with irresponsible actions (“falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic”, Schenck v United States, 1917). Vaccine mandates are as American as apple pie and ... George Washington. According to the Washington Post, “There is a long history of mandatory immunizations supported by American leaders. After seeing how the disease had ravaged American forces, George Washington instructed an army doctor in Philadelphia to begin administering “inoculation” to the soldiers – a controversial method of immunization in the 1700s in which patients developed mild cases of smallpox before becoming immune. “I have determined that the troops shall be inoculated,” Washington wrote in February 1777. “Necessity not only authorizes but seems to require the measure, for should the disorder infect the Army in the natural way and rage with its usual virulence, we should have more to dread from it than from the Sword of the Enemy.” “The smallpox epidemic killed more than 100,000 people between 1775 and 1782. While the measure was not popular among soldiers, there is no evidence of mass refusal against immunization, according to the Library of Congress.” “The issue of mandatory vaccinations in the United States made its way to the Supreme Court in the early 1900s, when a smallpox vaccination law in Cambridge, Mass., was challenged by a man who refused to comply. Massachusetts had led the nation in passing vaccine law, but Henning Jacobson, a pastor, said his refusal to be vaccinated against smallpox was a personal decision. “In a February 1905 decision, the Supreme Court ruled 7 to 2 that public health could supersede individual rights. “[T]he liberty secured by the Constitution of the United States to every person within its jurisdiction does not import an absolute right in each person to be, at all times and in all circumstances, wholly free from restraint,” Justice John Marshall Harlan wrote for the majority. “There are manifold restraints to which every person is necessarily subject for the common good.” “The Supreme Court recently declined to take up a case challenging a vaccine mandate at Indiana University. Justice Amy Coney Barrett who received the request because she is the Supreme Court justice tasked with reviewing emergency petitions from that region of the country, did not give a reason for the high court’s declining to block the mandate.” So, if you are refusing to get vaccinated because of your individual rights and freedoms, you are the one who is being un-American. –Andy Wasserman is a Piedmont resident. 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmontpost.org Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall City Editor: Allyson Aleksey PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Jay Russell Ed Gilligan SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. articles.text: Well, football season is in full swing. but this year Bay Area fans don‘t have much to cheer about. I guess we have to go nostalgic and remember past glories. Or at least some fun stories. I remember hearing about a very unusual Cotton Bowl game in 1954. The University of Alabama was playing Rice University. It was Rice all the way. The partisan Texas crowd was cheering wildly. The Alabama team and the fans who made it to Texas for the Cotton Bowl were pretty glum. Alabama half back Tommy Lewis was terribly frustrated as he sat there on the bench watching Rice roll up one touchdown after another. Then something happened that made the Cotton Bowl of 1954 a memorable event. A Rice All-American halfback took the ball on his own 5-yard line and headed down the sideline toward the Crimson Tide goal line. When he reached Alabama’s 38-yard line – directly in front of the Alabama bench and Lewis – the Alabama back could no longer contain himself. He leaped from the sideline and tackled the ball carrier. They gave Rice the touchdown! (It’s on YouTube). I’ve often wondered what happened to that young halfback who cared so much that he could not contain himself. His judgment may have been poor, but you can redirect that kind of zest for living and make it constructive and creative. It would be misleading for me to suggest to you that all of our days will be exciting and happy. Many of them will be just regular days. articles.text: Thomas Krolczyk is the newest officer to join the Piedmont Police Department, officially joining on August 24 from Broadmoor Police Department in Daly City. He has worked for departments in several Bay Area communities, beginning as a community service officer with the Ceres Police Department in 2007. He then moved to the Hayward Police Department where he worked as a Reserve Police Officer for four years before becoming a full-time officer at Broadmoor PD for two years. He is an academy graduate of Evergreen Valley College, and is a member of FALEO, the Filipino American Law Enforcement Officers Association. He received a Chief of Police Award in April 2021 from the Broadmoor Police Department for outstanding police work. When considering the move from Broadmoor to Piedmont, he said he was especially intrigued by the various similarities between the departments and the communities they serve. “I came from a very small community in Broadmoor, but a very well-educated and influential community that was extremely supportive of its police department,” Krolczyk said. “The department and community had a great relationship.” Originally from Fremont, Krolczyk said he was very familiar with Piedmont before joining the department. “I told myself, if I ever transition [from Broadmoor], it would be to a department in Alameda County and in a small agency. There really aren’t many small agencies in the East Bay and Piedmont is one of them, so I started doing my research,” he said. Officer Thomas Krolczyk Krolcyzk added that even in his first week he noticed similarities between the two departments and communities, making for a comfortable transition. Prior to policing, Krolcyzk was a small business owner. He owned a barbershop in Danville in Blackhawk. Despite the obvious differences between policing and barbering, Krolcyzk said he gained skills in customer service as a small business owner that he uses on the force today. “People expect a certain level of customer service, and I take pride knowing the shop was rated highly for its service. I grew my business within a small community, so when I first joined Piedmont, it instantly felt like home,” he said. hours.

articles.text: The gubernatorial recall election of Gov. Gavin Newsom has failed. The Associated Press made the announcement less than one hour after polls closed on Tuesday, September 14. Gov. Newsom is the second governor in U.S history to defeat a recall, aimed at removing an elected official from office before their term expires. It was pegged by other Democrats as a GOP-led recall. President Joe Biden, Vice President Kamala Harris, and House Speaker Nancy Pelosi all threw their support behind the governor leading up to the election. “I am humbled and grateful to the millions, and millions of Californians who exercised their fundamental right to vote, and express themselves so overwhelmingly by rejecting the division,” he said when delivering remarks from Sacramento following the results.
articles.title: Recall fails, Newsom remains governor

articles.text: The Wellness Center Support Committee has announced the second annual Walk for Wellness, the largest yearly fundraiser for the Wellness Center located at Piedmont High School. The event will take place September 20-26, and is an inclusive, accessible and socially-distanced event open to the entire Piedmont community. Co-chaired by Nicki Gilbert and KeriAnne Hohener, it focuses on physical, mental and emotional wellness. “Walk for Wellness raises much-needed funding for the Wellness Center while increasing awareness of the need for mental health services for students,” said Hohener. Last year’s walk raised over $37,000. “Our goal is to exceed the amount this year. Our students’ health and wellness is clearly a priority for our community,” said Gilbert. Participants will receive fun giveaways and access to a choice of maps detailing walks around town. Participants are invited to collect their giveaways at the Walk for Wellness booth at the Harvest Festival on September 19. All Piedmonters are encouraged to gather their families, friends and pets and participate in as many walks as possible during the week of September 20, and to post photos from their walks on Instagram (@piedmontwellness). The PUSD Wellness Center provides confidential, free on-campus and online counseling to all Piedmont High School, Millennium High School and Piedmont Middle School students. The Wellness Center helps students manage common emotional and social challenges of middle and high school including stress, depression, grief, family or friendship conflicts, and substance use concerns. Approximately one third of high school and one quarter of middle school students receive counseling at the Wellness Center each year. The Walk for Wellness Committee is grateful to more than 30 Piedmont families who are sponsoring the event, and to corporate and in-kind sponsors. articles.text: On August 24 Piedmont School District announced the formation of a COVID Health and Safety Steering Committee. It consists of 10 members, including district administrators, school board members, and nurses, plus seven medical professionals from the community, including Epidemiologist Dr. George Rutherford. The committee has met twice, on August 25 and September 8, and will continue meeting at least to the end of the year. The Committee’s opinions and information will be sent to Superintendent Randy Booker, who will advise to the school board. The meetings are private and not open to the public. All meetings will be held virtually, follow an agenda and include time for anyone to bring up any concerns. “These types of Committees are valuable for providing different perspectives to assist District staff in making decisions and recommendations. The return to full, in-person instruction, while dealing with the Delta variant, made bringing the Committee back together an easy decision,” explained Communications Director Brian Killgore. Last year, the first version of the committee worked behind the scenes to transition to distance learning and to develop the hybrid schedule when classes returned at a limited capacity. articles.text: Climate Equity and Environmental Justice Dept to be interdisciplinary UC Berkeley’s new interdisciplinary Climate Equity and Environmental Justice faculty cluster is, from left, Meg Mills-Novoa, Daniel Aldana Cohen, Maya Carrasquillo, Danielle Zoe Rivera and Zoé Hamstead. [Photo by Brittany Hosea-Small] University of California, Berkeley has introduced a new Climate Equity and Environmental Justice faculty, as part of six interdisciplinary faculty “cluster hires” currently underway on campus. The group includes Meg Mills-Novoa, Daniel Aldana Cohen, Maya Carrasquillo, Danielle Zoe Rivera and Zoé Hamstead. Cluster hiring is an emerging practice in universities across the country, which involves the appointment of multiple scholar of field experts based on shared research interests. “[These] intellectual clusters share the goal of advancing knowledge about how to address acute threats to the world, particularly to its vulnerable and marginalized populations,” said Raka Ray, dean of Berkeley’s Division of Social Sciences. “Berkeley has always had an interest in and a belief in cross-disciplinary initiatives, and they’ve usually been done through centers and institutes,” said Ray, a sociologist, who is overseeing four of the six cluster hires. Ben Hermalin, vice provost for the faculty, added that concern about the diversity of Berkeley’s current faculty, in terms of their areas of research, as well as race, gender and ethnicity, was a “major factor” in choosing cluster hires to broaden the professoriate on campus. “Higher education hasn’t been diverse in its topics of inquiry, its academic pursuits,” he said. “It’s been too Eurocentric, too focused on the issues of people who are doing relatively well. Populations have gotten neglected.” The University is advancing interdisciplinary research by hiring professors and researchers in five key areas: Native American and Indigenous People, Anti-Black Racism and Social Inclusion, Latinx and Democracy, Artificial Intelligence and Inequality, and Understanding Non-citizenship.
articles.title: UC Berkeley hires faculty members for new program

[Photo by Brittany Hosea-Small] By Allyson Aleksey University of California, Berkeley has introduced a new Climate Equity and Environmental Justice faculty, as part of six interdisciplinary faculty “cluster hires” currently underway on campus. The group includes Meg Mills-Novoa, Daniel Aldana Cohen, Maya Carrasquillo, Danielle Zoe Rivera and Zoé Hamstead. Cluster hiring is an emerging practice in universities across the country, which involves the appointment of multiple scholar of field experts based on shared research interests. “[These] intellectual clusters share the goal of advancing knowledge about how to address acute threats to the world, particularly to its vulnerable and marginalized populations,” said Raka Ray, dean of Berkeley’s Division of Social Sciences. “Berkeley has always had an interest in and a belief in cross-disciplinary initiatives, and they’ve usually been done through centers and institutes,” said Ray, a sociologist, who is overseeing four of the six cluster hires. Ben Hermalin, vice provost for the faculty, added that concern about the diversity of Berkeley’s current faculty, in terms of their areas of research, as well as race, gender and ethnicity, was a “major factor” in choosing cluster hires to broaden the professoriate on campus. “Higher education hasn’t been diverse in its topics of inquiry, its academic pursuits,” he said. “It’s been too Eurocentric, too focused on the issues of people who are doing relatively well. Populations have gotten neglected.” The University is advancing interdisciplinary research by hiring professors and researchers in five key areas: Native American and Indigenous People, Anti-Black Racism and Social Inclusion, Latinx and Democracy, Artificial Intelligence and Inequality, and Understanding Non-citizenship. articles.text: As humans worldwide share their joy and excitement behind the Space Renaissance’s resurgence, space sustainability becomes increasingly important. Since the launch of the first satellite, Sputnik 1, in 1957, humankind has carried out over 4,700 launches. That number keeps rising, and we are now seeing Earth’s lower orbit become dangerously congested. What is space debris? Space debris is made up of all the things humans send to space that previously weren’t there, including all rockets, satellites, and space stations. It won’t stop here. Once something is sent to space, it stays. It is natural for anything to break down over time and these spacecrafts are no exception. Any chipped paint, broken antennas, and fragments from satellite collisions contribute to the growing space debris crisis. Speed moves differently in space. While it appears unlikely that chipped paint or a broken antenna will do much damage, it travels faster than a speeding bullet that can do some serious damage to spacecraft. How much is out there? As of 2019, we know of over 23,000 fragments of large-scale space debris. Scientists have uncovered this because these pieces are visible, making them easier to track. The more daunting items are smaller, non-visible fragments. These are fragments of space debris between 0.4-4 inches. It is estimated that they total 500,000 fragments. Why does it matter? It is important to view space as an ecosystem that needs protection. When we regard space in this matter, we can consider the carbon footprint we are leaving on it. As of now, no one can really speak about the long-term impact or consequences of leaving behind the amount of space debris we have floating around. Th debris stays in space because there is no removal or retrieval process. If a satellite falls into Earth’s orbit, usually it will burn away in the Earth’s atmosphere, but not every time. What is being done? There are known cases of satellite rubble crashing on Earth. In space, the International Space Station (ISS) must stay alert for any collisions. There are protoCredit: JanieCBros cols in place if they see something in their trajectory. Even then, there is nothing to prevent the smaller fragments damaging the bodies of active spacecraft. Satellites could crash into each other, disrupting communication and navigation systems. Aside from the destruction of these satellites, collisions add more debris to the growing problem. As space travel is expected to increase, scientists are working to ensure a clear, safe path for entering orbit. If there is too much congestion, launches cannot occur safely. There are proposals and ideas with different strategies for tackling space debris. A Japanese satellite company proposed ELSA-D, short for end-of-life services. The goal is to use a satellite and magnetic system to safely capture objects. This technology is still new, and it is unclear how effective it is to larger spacecraft. Our efforts are best spent on finding ways to have sustainable space experiences so that we can continue our exhibitions of space. articles.text: A work crew from the Oaks League at the Cascades at Joaquin Miller Park. During the dangerously hot and dry summer months, the f ledgling Piedmont/Oakland chapter of Boys Team Charity League identified fire safety as a project focus. Under the leadership of board member, Christina Vo, the Oaks League took on the gargantuan task of identifying and partnering with local organizations in need of help, educating itself and others within the community on salient issues related to fire safety and preparedness, and “walking the walk” by rolling up its sleeves to take action. As has been made apparent to this generation, most recently by the devastation caused by last year’s Glass Fire in Napa and now the Caldor Fire in Tahoe, fire season is upon us and will continue to rage if not controlled. Clearing overgrown space in and around the community – as well as around your own home – can do much to help prevent disaster. So far, the boys and their parents have logged over 60 volunteer hours with partners at North Hills Association, Friends of Joaquin Miller Park, and Friends of Sausal Creek. The League is learning much from stories of previous generations. Sue and Gordon Piper with the North Hills Association survived the Firestorm in 1991, when they lost their home. Both have dedicated their time clearing the brush, advocating with local government agencies to keep everyone safe from fires, and teaching the public about ways to protect themselves and their homes. They developed the Firestorm Memorial Garden and the Gateway Emergency Preparedness Exhibit Center & Garden at the base of Hiller Highlands to assist in these efforts. The Boys Team Charity Oaks League teammates have cleared weeds and fire danger plants from the hills above Highway 13 at both locations. The group has spread literally a ton of compost to feed the native plants that grow there and prepared the garden for a memorial dedication. In Joaquin Miller Park, six boys and their families cleaned out the Cascades under the direction of Dale Risden, a neighbor of the park who plans to have a grand re-opening of the Cascades in early October. Due to neglect over the years from drought, the pool of water was filled with large sticks, trash and muck. It was quite a testament to teamwork watching some of the Oaks League members wade through the muck to pull out the debris while others carried it away from the area. All of the upcoming Boys Team Charity Oaks League meetings this fall will focus on fire safety and preparedness. They recently worked with the Piedmont Fire Department to learn how to help families build an evacuation plan, identify a meeting spot, make a home video to record contents and upload it to the cloud, as well as compile a short and prioritized list of evacuation essentials. If you are interested in joining League and working side-byside with your son doing good within your own community, keep an eye out for the Oaks League open enrollment in January. articles.text: Piedmont’s varsity football team lost its season opener 29-21 to Durham on Friday, September 10 at Witter Field. The shorthanded Highlanders, with only six substitute players, held a 13-6 lead with 7:34 left in the third quarter but watched it dwindle away as fatigue affected the starting players, most of whom were playing both on both offense and defense. The Highlanders entered the game without having played any scrimmages. “We knew we’d have some hiccups with a scrimmage. It was the first time we had live action against anybody,” said coach Jerome Johnson. “We now have to go back, break down everything that happened on film, and build from it.” “With low numbers of players, kids were cramping up. It’s a constant grind and they know it’s all about conditioning physically and mentally. I’m proud of everyone,” added Johnson. Saturday’s game featured Nina Goldberg as the team’s kicker and first female player to score points for the team in more than 10 years. Goldberg, a senior, was recruited from the soccer team, where she has been a starter since her freshman year. In Friday’s football game, she converted a PAT kick to put Piedmont ahead 13-6 in the second quarter. “I’m proud of Nina,” said coach Johnson. “Next week, hopefully we’ll get more touchdowns and have her try a few more.” Game summary Both teams traded possessions that ended with punts until Piedmont began a drive with 10:18 left in the second quarter. Starting at its own 21-yard line, Piedmont held onto the ball for seven minutes resulting in a touchdown. On the drive, PHS converted a 3rd and 11 from their own 20 when quarterback Nico Defazio connected with Mateo Costa for a 32 yard reception at Durham’s 48 yard line. Then on 3rd and 10 from the 48, Defazio hit Lucas Bernales on a 22-yard dart over the middle to the 26. But faced with a 3rd down and 32 yards to go for a first down, Defazio found Ryan McConathy on an 18-yard pass. On 4th down and 12, Evan McConathy. The twin brother of Ryan, grabbed a 15-yard reception. With a first down at the 14-yard line. Defazio hit a sneaky read-option keeper for a touchdown. The extra point attempt was missed, 6-0. The Trojans scored quickly with a 60-yard touchdown on the second play. Piedmont’s defense blocked the PAT, and the score remained tied, 6-6. Piedmont started the third quarter with an interception by Battista Costa at the Trojans’ 26 yard line, Defazio hit Evan McConathy with a perfect pass on a streak down the right side for Piedmont’s second touchdown. The receiver came down with a jostling catch, trapping the ball with one hand against his helmet and quickly securing with his second hand as he hit the ground. Goldberg then knocked the ball through the uprights for a 13-6 lead. After Piedmont forced another punt to their own 9-yard line, the wheels seemingly began to fall off. On 4th-and-11 at their own six, PHS’ punt attempt went out the back of the end zone for a safety, 13-8. Paying safety on defense, Defazio, reeled in an interception in the third quarter, but the offense was stalled. PHS punted quickly and Durham was able to Photo by Mark Aikawa Piedmont receiver Evan McConathy (5) makes a leaping touchdown reception against Durham. Photo by Mark Aikawa Nina Goldberg kicks a PAT (point after touchdown) in the third quarter in Piedmont’s season-opening game with Durham. Photo by Jeff Smet Nico Defazio makes an interception against Durham on Friday, September 1- at Witter Field. score from their own 36-yard line on a long catch and run, making it 16-13 in favor of the Trojans with 3:42 left in the third quarter. After another punt, Durham started its drive at Piedmont’s 43-yard line. They drove to the one-yard line and punched it across for a 22-13 lead with 10:19 left in the fourth quarter after Ethan Feldstein’s second blocked PAT of the game. Durham scored its fourth touchdown at 7:21 for a 29-13 lead. But the Highlanders had more to say. Starting at their own 45, they driving to Durham’s one-yard line with a 39-yard pass to Lucas Bernales. Defazio pushed it across the goal line on a quarterback plunge, then made a 2-point conversion on another pass to Bernales, and closed the score to 29-21 with 3:06 left. An onside kick was fielded cleanly by Durham, which then ran out the clock for the victory. Official stats were not available by press time. articles.text: Photos by Brian Mahany At No. 1 doubles, Amanda Becker (left) and Audrey Mahany went 2-1 at a tournament at James Logan in Union City. Playing without Bridgette McEfee, its No. 1 singles player, Piedmont’s tennis team won half of its four matches last weekend at the James Logan Tournament on Friday and Saturday, September 10-11. With a 2-2 record, they placed third in the consolation bracket. The team was scheduled to face Acalanes in the first round, but the Dons never showed up, resulting in a win by forfeit for PHS. In the next round Piedmont lost 5-2 to Irvington. On Saturday, the Highlanders lost 6-1 to Campolindo but followed up with a 4-3 win over league rival Berkeley on Saturday. “We took bronze consolation ladder without our No. 1 singles starter, Bridgette McEfee. We had some close matches against Irvington despite losing 5-2, and fared much better in Round 2 against our league rivals [Berkeley]. The win got us third. We also played Cal High in a non-tournament match,” said coach Jim Landes. The Highlanders defeated Berkeley by sweeping all three doubles matches and N 4 singles. Berkeley was not able to field a No. 4 singles starter. 4-3 win over Berkeley Doubles players only played a single eight-point set in the tournament. Piedmont’s 4-3 team over Berkeley featured all three doubles teams winning their matches: No. 1 Amanda Becker and Audrey Mahany won 8-5, Mara LaForte and Rose Siemers at No. 2 won 8-3, while Ceci Defazio and Emma Eisemon swept to an 8-0 victory. At singles, No. 1 Anne Jumper lost to Yellowjackets’ Maya Curry 6-2, 6-3, and No. 2 Michaela Bini lost 6-0, 6-0. Anika Gilliland at No. 3, lost a heated three-set match, 7-5, 4-6, 10-8. “Anne Jumper played very well against Curry, who is a very good player. Anika lost by a very narrow margin. Corey (Reich – assistant coach) and I were very proud of the way Anika competed on both days,” said Landes. Against Campolindo, Piedmont’s only win came from LaForte and Siemers at No. 2 doubles, 8-4. The two other doubles matches were close as well, Becker and Mahany lost a close 8-6 battle, while the No. 3 duo Audrey Frankel and Sofia Ferraro went an extra point, 9-7. Singles losses: Jumper (6-1, 6-0), Bini (6-0, 6-1), Gilliland (6-2, 6-0), Eisemon (6-3, 6-0). 5-2 loss to Irvington Against Irvington of Fremont, Becker and Mahany came away with a commanding 8-1 win. Senior Jack Stein picked up where he left off last season, finishing sixth of 174 runners with a time of 14:36 on the 2.9-mile course. He trailed 30 runners at one point, but progressively picked up the pace to a sixthplace finish. “It was a great race,’ Stein said. “The first race is always a bit nerve-wracking. I had around 30 runners in front of me at the beginning, and my strategy was to start picking them off one by one,” said Stein. Stein emerged last season as a standout with consistent competitive times in both cross-country and 1,600- and 3,200-meters in track. The boys’ team hasn’t qualified for the State meet since 2017, also with Proctor. articles.text: Tara Kothari (14) is a bright spot for PHS volleyball. She had 14 kills and two serving aces against Encinal. When we’re at our best, we’re moving around and being unpredictable,” she added. The Jets were one of two teams Piedmont beat last season, including a marathon victory in five sets last spring. articles.text: Photos courtesy of AmericanSoccerNow.com Ricardo Pepi scored in the 75th minute against Honduras on Wednesday, September 8 to help the U.S. Men’s Soccer Team to win 4-1. The first three matches of 14 matches in the 2022 FIFA World Cup Qualifies have been played, and the U.S. Men’s National Team sits with one win and two ties (1-2-0), holding a qualification spot with five points. It drew 0-0 with El Salvador on September 2, then tied Canada 1-1 on September 5. It got its first win on September 8, a comfortable 4-1 victory over Honduras on September 8. The Nil-Nil draw with El Salvador came in a mesmerizing game with a packed house of 30,000. The 1-1 draw with Canada, played in Nashville, didn’t offer much home team support. Both matches were hampered by Sergino Dest sustaining an injury, and Weston McKennie being sent packing back to Italy after violating team rules. However, the United States turned the tide with its 4-1 win in Honduras. The U.S. trailed Honduras 1-0 after 27 minutes but tied in the 48th. Ricardo Pepi got the go-ahead in the 75th, then the flood gates opened with goals at 86 minutes by Brenden Aaronson and in stoppage time by Sebastian Lletget. The first two draws left a bit more to be desired after the United States had won a pair of trophies this summer, the Nations League on June 6 and Gold Cup on August 1. Both were victories over longtime nemesis Mexico. The Stars and Stripes’ next matches are October 7 against Jamaica in Austin, Texas; a game with Panama’s at its home field on October 10l and a final qualifying game on October 13 in Columbus, Ohio against Costa Rica. The U.S. is considered the favorite in all matches. Remember October 10, 2017, when the U.S. men lost 2-1 to Trinidad and Tobago and failed to qualify for the 2018 World Cup. This is a very important time for the team. The U.S. is good, perhaps the deepest and most talented it’s ever been. Since the 2017 defeat to Trinidad, the Yankees have produced a wealth of young stars. For instance, Christian Pulisic, age 22, is among the biggest stars in the Premier League with Chelsea; Weston McKennie, 23, is a starter for Juventus in Italy’s Serie A; Gio Reyna, 18, plays with Germany’s superclub Borussia Dortmund; and Tyler Adams, 22, is a star at RB Leipzig in Germany The best part? Only one regular starter for the U.S. is above 30, Tim Reem at 32. So, this current roster will also headline the 2026 World Cup in the United States, Canada, and Mexico (with Santa Clara’s Levi Stadium getting one of the matches). It was a frustrating start to World Cup Qualifiers for the U.S. after a 0-0 draw with El Salvador and 1-1 with Canada. Weston McKennie was sent home after the match for violating team rules. Can the U.S. Men’s National Team qualify for the 2022 World Cup? Now is the time to pay attention and find out.

articles.text: A retrospective art exhibit celebrating the pioneering feminist artist Judy Chicago is now on display at the de Young museum in San Francisco through January 9, 2022. Judy Chicago is one of the founding figures behind the 1970’s feminist art movement. Her storied career is highlighted through her colorful works on canvas, porcelain plates, car hoods and more. The exhibition will include approximately 130 paintings, prints, drawings and sculptures by the artist. The event is organized in conjunction with the 100th anniversary of women’s right to vote in the United States and pays homage to Judy Chicago who fought against the suppression of women’s creativity. She founded the first feminist arts education proFeminist artist Judy Chicago. gram in the country at California State University in Fresno. To purchase tickets to the exhibition, visit https://deyoung. famsf.org/exhibitions/judy-chicago. The de Young Museum in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park.

articles.text: Joan Mitchell, a comprehensive retrospective featuring over 80 distinguished works, had its world premiere at SF MOMA on September 4. The exhibition is co-organized with SF MOMA and the Baltimore Museum of Art and will be on display through January 17, 2022. As a painter Mitchell first attained significant acclaim in the 1950’s New York art scene, and found considerable success in the male-dominated, abstract expressionist circles during that time. Mitchell, originally from Chicago, then spent three decades in France honing her craft. Although she lived overseas for much of her career, she is considered one of the leading figures of the American abstract expressionist movement. Mitchell cites Paul Cezanne, Wassily Kandinsky, Henri Matisse, and Vincent Van Gogh as influences on her work. SF MOMA features a few of her paintings side-by-side, including a copy of a Van Gogh work, showing the similarities between the two painters. Her work, though abstract, resembles the Staff Photos To the Harbormaster, oil on canvas (1957). Joan Mitchell worked primarily in oil paints, on a primed canvas or white ground. many landscapes Mitchell has encountered - from Lake Michigan in Chicago, to the Hudson River in New York, and finally the riverbanks of France. Many of her paintings are large in scale, covering more than one canvas or panel. Noteworthy paintings include “The Bridge,” her first two-panel painting and a vivid work in dark hues, and “Girolata Triptych,” the artists’ first three-panel work inspired by the island of Corsica and drenched in blue-green and purple oil paints. She often painted with poetry in mind - another noteworthy, large painting, “To the Harbormaster,” is named after her friend Frank O’Hara’s poem. Visit SF MOMA to view the many artworks, sketchbooks, and drawings by Mitchell, now through January. Visit https://www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/joan-mitchell to purchase tickets. The world premiere at SF MOMA was co-organized with the Baltimore Museum of Art. Joan Mitchell is a comprehensive retrospective featuring over 80 works.
articles.title: World premiere of Joan Mitchell retrospective comes to SF MOMA

articles.text: Filoli House and Gardens in Woodside is celebrating “Orchard Days” every weekend from September 25 through October 31. articles.text: The Invisible Man is a riveting psychological thriller, and a reboot of the 1933 film based on the H.G. Wells 1897 novel of the same name. In this contemporary update, written and directed by Leigh Whannell, the story is filled with far more meaning and nuance than simply a sci-fi/horror tale; instead, in context and theme, it speaks to a far different audience about a subject that is of the moment. It’s extraordinarily good. In its first moments, the story achieves a tone of tension and menace. It’s the dead of night and a young woman, Cecilia Kass (Elizabeth Moss), lies awake, staring at a dimly lighted digital clock. Next to her is a man deeply asleep. She gingerly frees herself from his draped arm and slowly slips out of bed. Watching him closely, she leaves the bedroom, turning a hallway camera toward the bed, and quietly hurries down a long dark hallway. In another room she hurriedly dresses, fills a small bag with clothes, stops in an expansive space filled with computer screens and electronics and pauses to glance at one screen in particular; the man is still sleeping. As she makes her way toward the front door, she accidentally kicks a metal dog dish that loudly slides across the hardwood floor. She waits. All is quiet. Her escape, not without another loud mishap, is almost complete as she emerges from the woods and stands in the middle of a narrow road, waiting for a car to arrive. Time is of the essence. And finally, with her sister, Emily Kass (Harriet Dyer), behind the wheel, Cecilia barely manages to escape. The plan is that she will stay at a safe house, the home of her friend James Lanier (Aldis Hodge), a police detective, and his daughter, Sydney (Storm Reid). Gradually, as the days pass, the hyper-vigilant fear of expecting to be found begins to ease. But it isn’t until Emily arrives and tells her that her boyfriend, Adrian (Oliver Jackson-Cohen), a genius specializing in advanced optics, has committed suicide that Cecilia fully exhales and a shroud of anxiety begins to lift; she is transformed while sitting Elizabeth Moss stars in The Invisible Man. with her sister’s phone, reading the news story. At the urging of James and Emily she tells them what her life with Adrian had been like, the emotional and physical abuse unrelenting, his manic need to control her life, even her thoughts. But now it’s over. She soon receives a phone call from Adrian’s younger brother, Tom (Michael Dorman), a lawyer, asking for a meet, one in which he tells Cecilia and Emily that Adrian has left her $5 million of his estate. Cecilia has not only been liberated but she is now wealthy. And so concludes act one. But it’s also at this point that the audience knows that there is much more yet to be told. The only question begged is what awaits Cecilia, whose only wish is to regain the life she knew before the emotional abyss called Adrian. But this is a good place to stop giving you, the reader, any further semblance of a plot line. For what takes place in the next two acts must be viewed absent any hint of what will unfold other than to say that this story offers a far more complex narrative than is likely assumed. Of course, The Invisible Man is a creepy horror tale with some solid jumps. Yes, it’s all that. But it’s also a haunting and chilling metaphor for a reality so many abused women face, meaning this film exists in a context of today’s #MeToo movement. Indeed, men who physically and psychologically abuse women are indeed invisible, existing in that fearful, smothering silence and starkly painful truth which is endured by the victims. The raging horror is real, the threats palpable, and even when spoken, as Cecilia finds out, it is often met with doubt. The woman is not believed. In thinking about The Invisible Man, two movies come to mind. One is the 1944 Gaslight, starring Ingrid Bergman and Charles Boyer, wherein he malignantly sets out to convince his wife that what is occurring is only imagined (he turns down the gas lighted wall lamps and insists he sees no change), his purpose being to manipulate and control her and make her doubt her own sanity. Hence the term “gaslighting.” The second film is Sleeping With the Enemy, a 1991 American psychological thriller starring Julia Roberts and Patrick Bergin. She is a physically and psychologically abused woman who is convinced by him that his outbursts are her fault. Like Cecilia, she plans an elaborate escape, terrified that he will find and harm her. Both of the films possess a sense of sinister apprehension that increases until the characters finally says, loudly and emphatically, “I see you,” and what was invisible is suddenly exposed. It’s a moment that is liberating and empowering. Of course, The Invisible Man has such a moment when Cecelia finally confronts her sadistic boyfriend, an encounter that results in an unexpected but just climax. She sees him. And then, with a smile, is finally able to look away. The Invisible Man. Directed by Leigh Whannell. Starring Elizabeth Moss, Harriet Dyer, Aldis Hodge. 2 hrs., 4 min. Rated R.

articles.text: Brie Larson and Jacob Tremblay star in Room. Room is a perplexing and riveting film, constructed in two acts. Know that act one is not only seemingly surreal, but increasingly difficult to watch. Not because it’s gratuitous, but because the reality endured by a young woman, Joy (Brie Larson), is grim and all but unimaginable. The film opens with Joy, also known as Ma, and her 5-year-old son, Jack (Jacob Tremblay), baking a birthday cake. They live in a detached, starkly furnished garden shed, roughly 10X10. Joy has been there for seven years. Jack knows no other world. The only source of light is a skylight that tells them when it rains, or when the sun shines. They are imprisoned, trapped behind a steel door by a middle-aged man known only as Nick (Sean Bridgers). He brings them food and uses Joy as sexual chattel (hence the birth of Jack). The first hour of Room (which is how Jack refers to the interior of the shed – not “the room” but simply “room”) is claustrophobic and psychologically chilling. Their survival is testimony to the resilience of Joy and Jack who have only each other and have, against all odds, adapted. But now that Jack is five, Joy can begin to contemplate a scenario that will at the very least free Jack. The events she sets in motion are harrowing and breathtaking and the stakes are impossibly high for both of them. Of course, it’s possible to think of this room as a metaphor. Life can feel like it has no exit and there are no viable options. And it is this sense of existential confinement that contributes to the unrelenting dread that the film conveys and sustains. The overwhelming question, from the first setup, is can Joy find a way out? Alone, without Jack, perhaps. But the thought of leaving him behind is unthinkable. The performances of Larson and Tremblay are both remarkable. The film resonates with their mother-son connection, one that seems natural while fraught with tension. Larson never lets her character slip into the melodramatic; rather, Joy faces a situation absent any histrionics. And Tremblay amazes. He is a kid, a wonderful, difficult, sweet kid who never falters in his portrayal of Jack. A final comment about films that are shot in a confined space, often called container films. Think of the room as a panic room, of sorts. A space from which the characters cannot leave. The issues confronting them seem more intense. Screenwriters of Sci-fi long ago discovered that to place a crew inside a spacecraft, to include a predatory alien, can be very effective. In a sense it’s a waterfall of emotions, which defines Room. Room. Directed by Larry Abrahamson. Starring Brie Larson, Jacob Tremblay, Sean Bridgers. 1 hr., 51 min. Rated R.

articles.text: A scene from The Secret Life of Pets. The Secret Lives of Pets is set initially in the New York apartment complex of Katie (Ellie Kemper), who lives with her Jack Russell terrier, Max (C.K.). But as we soon discover, the building is a menagerie of domesticated pets, and Max, being the gregarious mutt that he is, socializes with his neighbors. There’s Chloe (Lake Bell), an obese, finicky tabby cat; Mel (Bobby Moynihan), a hardcharging pug; Buddy (Hannibal Burgess), a likable miniature dachshund; Sweet Pea, a yellow and blue parakeet; and a snowwhite Pomeranian named Gidget (Jenny Slate). The story begins in earnest when Katie decides Max could use some company and brings home an oversized, Newfoundland schlub of a pooch she calls Duke (Eric Stonestreet). Naturally Max and Duke have issues. And it’s at this point that the premise of the story is fully revealed: what do animals do all day while their owners are at work? Of course, it will be one adventure after the next, involving lots of New York animals that they meet along the way. Some, such as Snowbal (Kevin Hart), are decidedly not domesticated. He is the leader of a gang of free-range rabbits. There’s a carnivorous Hawk, a pig with tattoos, and a Bassett hound named Pops (Dana Carvey). What gets everything going is that while Duke and Max are on a daily outing with their dog walker, they decide to make a break for it. But before long the two are captured by the Animal Control workers, and off they go to the pound. And so begins an improbable journey by the two amigos, starting with their escape from behind bars. The tale is now about their struggle to return home, meaning Ellie’s apartment. Meanwhile, to keep things interesting, Gidget and crew are in the hunt for the missing duo, and are having their own problems navigating the streets of New York. It’s a frenetic tale, and the kids will find the lineup of animals perpetually delightful. By Chris Honoré The Secret Lives of Pets is set initially in the New York apartment complex of Katie (Ellie Kemper), who lives with her Jack Russell terrier, Max (C.K.). But as we soon discover, the building is a menagerie of domesticated pets, and Max, being the gregarious mutt that he is, socializes with his neighbors. There’s Chloe (Lake Bell), an obese, finicky tabby cat; Mel (Bobby Moynihan), a hardcharging pug; Buddy (Hannibal Burgess), a likable miniature dachshund; Sweet Pea, a yellow and blue parakeet; and a snowwhite Pomeranian named Gidget (Jenny Slate). The story begins in earnest when Katie decides Max could use some company and brings home an oversized, Newfoundland schlub of a pooch she calls Duke (Eric Stonestreet). Naturally Max and Duke have issues. And it’s at this point that the premise of the story is fully revealed: what do animals do all day while their owners are at work? Of course, it will be one adventure after the next, involving lots of New York animals that they meet along the way. Some, such as Snowbal (Kevin Hart), are decidedly not domesticated. He is the leader of a gang of free-range rabbits. There’s a carnivorous Hawk, a pig with tattoos, and a Bassett hound named Pops (Dana Carvey). What gets everything going is that while Duke and Max are on a daily outing with their dog walker, they decide to make a break for it. But before long the two are captured by the Animal Control workers, and off they go to the pound. And so begins an improbable journey by the two amigos, starting with their escape from behind bars. The tale is now about their struggle to return home, meaning Ellie’s apartment. Meanwhile, to keep things interesting, Gidget and crew are in the hunt for the missing duo, and are having their own problems navigating the streets of New York. It’s a frenetic tale, and the kids will find the lineup of animals perpetually delightful. articles.text: Healthy Landscapes event sponsored by Piedmont Connect Piedmont Connect will host another Healthy Landscapes Front Garden Tour for one week, from Saturday, September 25 through Sunday, October 3. articles.text: In vino veritas – in wine there is truth. Every gourmet knows this famous adage. Sorry Zenobio, you should have said In musico veritas. My reasoning is simple. Can you trust a drunk to tell the truth? Not likely. But music speaks from the heart. No commentator is needed. All musical performance is autobiographical. Abraham Lincoln said that we cannot escape history. If Lincoln were writing about musicians, he might have said: “we cannot escape ourselves.“ For there is truth in every performance. Your true personality is always revealed. It needs to be said that “In Musico Veritas” applies only to acoustical instruments, including the human voice. All bets are off with amplified instruments. The amplification machine has no emotion. The soul is revealed in acoustic music. In order to appreciate these truths, the listener must tune in and look deep into the soul of the performer. Don’t be fooled by theatrics. Truth be told, the more theatrics on stage the shallower the performer. Mugging for the audience is not emotion… And how about smashing the instruments on stage after the concert. What does this reveal? The beauty of music is that there are unlimited possibilities. Psychoanalysis goes only so far. Bing Crosby was right when he said, “The difference of opinion is what makes horse racing.” And also with music. And now for something completely different America was famous for its concert bands. The Sousa band and the Gilmore bands were two of the most famous. Band concerts were popular with the general public. It was fun to be there. But don’t fool yourself. The concerts had a bit of everything. The public had fun and they learned a lot. Piedmont relived some of that nostalgia at the Piedmont Center for the Arts last Saturday at noon. The Renegade Orchestra played on the lawn. The weather was perfect and Renegade found a way to please every musical taste. To state the obvious, the diversity of entertainment at the PCA is astonishing. And if you missed it, come back: there will be much more coming.

articles.text: Piedmont violinist Joseph Gold celebrated his 75th birthday with a lovely concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Seventy-five is an interesting number. It has a round feel but is odd. It isn’t divisible like 36 but it gets more respect. To a gemologist, 75 is a diamond… clear, regular, but hard. It does glitter. 75 often comes with white hair. That kind of sets off the face like white icing on a birthday cake. 75 is a slow race to 100. It reminds me of the glorious finish to the first sub four-minute mile by Roger Bannister. He collapsed at the finish line. Maybe 75 just feels better. I don’t want to collapse. The day itself was a condensation of life. I awoke just before 5 a.m. –which coincidently was the hour of my birth. A good breakfast and some study and reflection on a good life. Then the concert - a brilliant affair with the auditorium filled to capacity. Friends both old and new and beautiful family. They do great honor to me, and I love them in return. The concert was like life itself. There were a few rough places and some glorious playing…reflecting a life of study, and a lot of good fortune. Thanks for a good family, friends and mentors and great composers and violin makers. All these bring on great sentiment. The presents were great but the best present of all is loving you. Thank you all.
articles.title: Reflections at 75

articles.text: Part 28 in a series In our age, when an architect lays out a building, the entire process starts with parking. With few exceptions, it is the driver for virtually all site and building design. The larger the building, and the more restrictive the municipal parking requirements, the more obvious this becomes. It follows that the cost, space requirements, and aesthetic influence of parking has a huge, often restrictive impact on denser multi-family housing. Factoring in aisle space and landscaping, a surface parking lot takes a lot of space — about 350 sf per car, while a tightly designed parking garage uses about 325 sf per car. Costs depend on specific site conditions but range from say, $5000/car for an on-grade parking lot to $50,000/car, and even more for underground parking. All of this must be factored into the housing costs, and paid for in the selling price or rent. This financial and spacial burden is a worldwide problem. In Japan for example, you have to prove you have a parking space before you are allowed to buy a car. There is a new attitude toward parking however that is becoming pervasive. It is the same concept that applies to the number of lanes provided on the freeway. Intuitively, it would seem that if traffic is clogged on the freeway, adding more lanes would solve the problem. Continuing studies have shown that the opposite is the case. In what is termed “induced traffic”, adding more lanes only ends up adding more cars, bringing the situation back to – or worse than – the original clogged condition. The same is true of parking: more parking induces more cars. For this reason, and because of the critical housing shortage, cities have started eliminating their minimum parking requirements. Zero is now the number of parking spaces required for new housing development in Berkeley, San Francisco, Mexico City, Minneapolis and many other places. The state of California now prohibits minimum parking requirements for ADU (accessory dwelling units). What does this mean for our built environment? Most of the older multi-family buildings in Piedmont that we showed in the last column have no onsite parking, with all tenant parking on the street. They were built in an age when people had fewer cars and walked to the Key System for a train ride to Oakland or San Francisco. This is a good example of showing that all planning systems are connected. Parking is linked to zoning, land use, transportation and availability of commercial services, all of which must work together to be viable. If household units live with one, or no cars, they must rely on walking, biking, public transportation, and ride sharing at least part of the time to get around. Fortunately, these alternatives can be immediately financed with the $800+ per month savings that AAA says the average person currently spends for car ownership, including parking. Next: Back to Aesthetics: Exterior Colors Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through Will@MakingDesignSense.com. The need for additional parking to accommodate our ever-increasing car ownership has led to a number of interesting solutions, such as this car lift system which allows double stacking – as opposed to simply parking everything in the front yard. The first question is, do we really need this many vehicles?

articles.text: The Montclair Lions Club and Montclair Village Association are collaborating to bring back the Restaurant Walk to Montclair Village. On Tuesday evening, September 28, from 6:00 to 8:30 p.m. A total of 14 merchants will open their doors and provide samples of their food and/or drink. Tickets to the event, called Passports, and can be purchased online at MontclairVillage.com, in advance at The Book Tree on La Salle Avenue, or in front of US Bank, 1998 Mountain Blvd., on the day of the event. The cost is $30, with proceeds going to support local non-profits, schools, and other worthy causes through the Lions Club. The Restaurant Walk also is an effort to bring some much-needed attention and patronage to the business owners of Montclair. The Montclair Lions Club will continue the tradition of supporting other service organizations and groups looking to raise some funds for their community work. Any organization wishing to sell a minimum of 10 tickets will receive 50% of the ticket proceeds. That’s $15 per ticket sold. For more information contact Leslie Masler with the Lions Club at 510-213-2530. New this year is the Wine and Beer Tasting Pavilion. Purchase a Wine and Beer Tasting package for an additional $25 and receive artisan wine pours from Wachira Wines, P. Harell Wines, R&B Cellars, and Montclair’s Perle Wine Bar and Bistro. Craft beers will be showcased by Taps and Takeout of Montclair. Wine and Beer tasting tickets are only available online and at the event. For advance tickets see MontclairVillage.com. The annual Restaurant Walk has been on pause for two years due to the COVID pandemic. For over 20 years this event has provided benefits to the Lions Club Centers for the Blind, the Leo Club at Oakland High School, and Montclair Lions Club Charities including Skyline High School, Montera Middle, Montclair, Joaquin Miller, and Thornhill Schools. The Montclair Lions Club supports local events like the Planter Mosaic program, Montclair Easter Egg Hunt, Annual Free Halloween Parade, and community cleanups. The Walk allows people to gather outdoors safely, support small businesses, and enjoy an evening tasting new menu items alongside Village favorites. This year a portion of the proceeds will go to provide financial relief to Montclair restaurants that suffered hardship due to the impacts of the COVID-19 virus. articles.text: “A Good Time Was Had By All” Last Sunday, September 12, Piedmont Community Church held its annual Homecoming Picnic in the courtyard at the Community Center. This event followed all Alameda County guidelines on health and safety relating to COVID 19. The church announced in advance that it would be held outdoors and casual attire was recommended. Interim Minister Dr. Steve Schibsted set an example for the entire congregation by preaching his sermon in shorts, which prompted Associate Pastor Don Ashburn to comment that this was a “first” in his 18 years at the church. The Music Aside from the spectacular weather, the greatest contributor to the festive atmosphere at the picnic was the outstanding music performed by Lodestar, a six-piece band consisting of: two Lance McCollum guitars (guitar aficionados will recognize the late builder of guitars with “piano-like” tone) played by band leader and singer James Haverkamp and Scott Fitzgerrell; Pam Bouey, violin; Russ Taylor, keyboard; Jim Semitekol, bass, and Harold Ohashi, drums. The band played a mix of music from artists such as the Everly Brothers, Paul Simon, Emmylou Harris, Linda Ronstadt and others. The Food A taco truck provided four types of soft tacos: pork, chicken, beef and vegetarian, made in advance, so the food line zipped along seamlessly. Freshly cut watermelon and cold lemonade were welcome on the warm September day. The quick lines left more time for people to have conversations and to get to know each other at the tables in the courtyard. A tribute to the quality of the food was that the 140 people consumed almost 400 tacos. The Games Beginning at noon kids and some intrepid adults played some games, including corn hole tournament, hula hoop challenge, water balloon toss, and old fashioned sack races. One little tyke decided the water balloon toss was meant for the intrusive cameraman, who was recording the games. An Invitation The Homecoming Picnic is an annual event which the Christian Education Board of the Piedmont Community Church sponsors, celebrating the end of summer and the beginning of a new church season as families return from vacations and their children return to school. This year’s event was truly enjoyable. Lodestar lead singer James Haverkamp engages the picnic audience of 140. Piedmont Church member Steve Senter enjoys the picnic under the brim of a hat.

articles.text: John St. John, 54, of Piedmont, California, died in a tragic auto accident in Le Sueur County, Minnesota on July 25, 2021. His beloved spouse Jill Davidson St. John, cherished daughter Claire Borgny St. John, and dear nephew Theo Emerson also passed away. He is survived by his treasured son Ryan St. John, loving mother and step-father Mary and Fritz Wooster of Piedmont, sisters Jane Emerson (Alex) and Molly Wooster, brother Tim Wooster (Jessica), nephew Ray Emerson, and aunt Julie St. John, who was near to his heart, and her husband Cliff Bream. John leaves behind his beloved and grieving in-laws Carey (Fred) Kaas, Shannon Davidson, and niece and nephew Kennedy and Keegan Kaas. Born in Minneapolis, Minnesota at the University of Minnesota Hospital on April 28, 1967, John spent most of his life in the Bay Area. He was proud of his East Bay identity. His mother, Mary, was 19 when he was born and they loved to tell people that they grew up together. His life was enriched when she married Fritz, whom he had known since his preschool days. His love for his new family was boundless. He was 13 when his sister Jane was born, followed by Tim less than two years later. Molly was born just before he graduated from high school. He was their big brother, their hero, their confidant, and their most beloved friend. John attended Beach School, was in the first graduating class from the new Piedmont Middle School, and graduated from Olympic Valley High School in Squaw Valley. It was there that he discovered his love of skiing and all sports requiring skill, athleticism, coordination, and an element of breath-taking risk. He was among the first to try the new sport known as snowboarding, but he truly found his bliss when downhill skiing. He was an expert water skier, kite boarder, wind surfer, electric skateboarder, and had only recently accepted the challenge of the electric unicycle. He felt most free when gliding, sometimes racing, along with the wind in his face and his body armored in the latest protective gear. After school John was a ski instructor in Squaw Valley and Steamboat Springs, Colorado. Finding a career that fit his skills and talents led him to form his own company, Cause Broadcasting. He created, produced, and sold public service announcements for college radio stations across the country. His gregarious personality was a perfect fit for his work. He truly tried to change the world for the better, one public service announcement at a time. Every client became a friend, and he enjoyed the relationships he created with college radio aficionados from San Francisco to Iowa City to the East Coast. John would proclaim to the world that marrying Jill Davidson and becoming father to Ryan and Claire were his finest achievements. His love for Jill was a delight to behold and he spent every free moment with her and Ryan and Claire. It was his good fortune that with Cause Broadcasting he created his own niche, which enabled him to work from home and always be at the ready should Jill or the children need a helping hand, a drive to Ryan’s drum lessons, Claire’s rehearsals, or just a good laugh. John’s sense of humor was legendary and no topic was too sacred to be spared his clever tongue. He was grateful to have a home in Piedmont, where he and his family built a wonderful community of friends. John was kind and generous and thoughtful. His presence will be missed by everyone who witnessed his cheerful greeting while out walking his dog, Casey. He considered every acquaintance to be a friend, and those of us who knew and loved him will hold his tender spirit forever. Donations in honor of the St. John family may be made to the Sierra Club or the SPCA.

articles.text: Jill Davidson St. John, 56, of Piedmont, California, died in a tragic auto accident in Le Sueur County, Minnesota on July 25, 2021. Her beloved spouse, John St. John; cherished daughter, Claire; and dear nephew, Theo, also passed away. She is survived by her treasured son, Ryan St. John; sisters, Shannon Davidson and Carey Davidson Kaas (Fred); Keegan and Kennedy Kaas; and her aunt Martha Geering-Kline (Bruce). Born in Berkeley, California on May 15, 1965, Jill created a beautiful, meaningful and full life in the Bay Area, continually inspired by its natural surroundings, vibrant culture and the people she loved. Jill was raised in Berkeley by parents Alan and Nancy Davidson. Alan was an attorney and marathon runner who charmed everyone with his humor, and Nancy approached life with kindness and understanding. Jill attended Albany High School, graduated from San Francisco State University, and earned a Master’s degree in Counseling/ Psychology from JFK University. Upon completing her Master’s degree and Marriage and Family Therapist License, she worked at Kaiser’s Chemical Dependency Program in Oakland, and later established her own practice in Lafayette, where she especially loved her work with teens and young adults. She helped countless friends and patients achieve a brighter life through sobriety. Jill’s sense of humor and intellectual curiosity enabled her to make people feel special, heard, and understood. She would look at you and you felt her unconditional love. Known for her positive outlook on life and faith, she was always eager to try new things and to reach out and connect with people. She was a health enthusiast, committed to running and exercise. When her husband was asked why he was marrying Jill, he said “because she makes everything fun.” She could be unpredictable, irreverent, and sometimes outrageous – always, always loving and kind. Nothing brought Jill more joy than raising her children with John. The deeply connected family enjoyed walking and skating in their neighborhood, exploring new places, laughing together, and sharing their love for music and animals. As a therapist, wife and mom, Jill encouraged that little be left unsaid in their home, and it was typically said loudly over Ryan’s drum practice in the basement, Claire’s singing preparing for a Berkeley Playhouse performance, and their dog Casey’s barking. All who were lucky enough to be blessed by Jill, John and Claire’s friendship and love will miss them dearly and will always hold a special place for them in their hearts and memories. Jill is predeceased by her loving parents, Alan and Nancy Davidson, as well as her aunt Sheila Geering Keppel (Jeff). She leaves behind her grieving and beloved in-laws Fritz and Mary Wooster, Jane, Alex and Ray Emerson, Tim and Jessica Wooster, Molly Wooster, and Julie St. John and her husband Cliff Bream.
articles.title: Jill St. John dies in fatal auto collision in Minnesota

articles.text: Claire Borgny St. John died at age 13 in a tragic auto accident in Le Sueur County, Minnesota on July 25, 2021. Her beloved parents, John and Jill St. John, and her cousin Theo Emerson also passed away. She is survived by her older brother, Ryan St. John, her grandparents, Mary and Fritz Wooster, and many loving uncles, aunts, and cousins. Claire was born in Oakland on February 7, 2008. She attended Wildwood Elementary School and Piedmont Middle School where she was known for her kindness, humor, fashion sense, and incredible talent as an actress and singer. Claire found joy in the performing arts, and successfully auditioned for roles in many live productions and then over Zoom during Covid. She had starring roles in Berkeley Playhouse productions and was proud to have played “Annie” at the Woodminster Amphitheatre. She truly shined each summer when she sang in the San Francisco Conservatory Music productions of Gilbert and Sullivan musicals. She was known for her eagerness to learn and grow, and for her kindness to the other musicians. She could play the ukulele and had the voice of an angel. She was a budding activist with a particular passion for Women’s Rights and, as a member of the Green Team, environmental issues. With Claire’s passing, the world has lost a delightful young woman with amazing potential. Claire found joy in everything: her family, friendships, music, animals, and nature. As her parents often said, “Claire just loves being Claire.” She had a clever sense of humor and a mature world view. She was kind, empathetic and passionate. Claire and her brother Ryan were especially close and loved family time with their parents and their family pets. They had the good fortune to travel to many places as a family: an RV trip to the national parks of southern Utah, to Minnesota, Hawaii, Sun Valley, Lake Tahoe, as well as Laguna Beach to visit her aunt Julie St. John. Claire was beloved by her cousins Keegan, Kennedy, Theo and Ray and spent many happy family holidays and vacations in their company. Claire will be remembered by all who were fortunate to know her for her vibrancy, her intelligence, her empathy, and her joy for life. To know Claire was to love her. She will be greatly missed. Jill and John St. John with daughter Claire.

articles.text: Theodore Fredrick Emerson passed away at age 9 in a tragic auto accident in Le Sueur County, Minnesota on July 25, 2021. Theo’s uncle, aunt and cousin (John, Jill and Claire St. John of Piedmont) also passed away. He is survived by his loving parents, Jane Wooster Emerson (PHS Class of 1998) and Alex Emerson, his younger brother Ray Emerson, both sets of grandparents (Fritz and Mary Wooster of Piedmont, CA and Dick and Susan Emerson of Redding, CT) and many loving aunts, uncles and cousins. Theo was born in Rochester, Minnesota on June 23, 2012, and lived his entire life in the Eagle Rock neighborhood of Los Angeles, California with his parents and brother. Theo attended Eagle Rock Elementary School. He loved school, his teachers and his classmates, and was especially proud of projects on the Miwok people of California and his Norwegian ancestry. Theo’s many interests outside of school included rock climbing, spending time in the woods with his friends, and shooting hoops in the backyard with his brother. This spring and summer, he attended Biocitizen hiking camp, rock climbing camp, and surf camp. He spent countless days at the beach where he was a bold and brave swimmer in big waves. One of his favorite places to spend summer days was a pool in Pasadena where he befriended the lifeguards and was happy to spend hours swimming, late into the evening. Theo was lucky to travel to Maine and Minnesota with extended family during summer vacations where he spent time with his beloved cousins. He also traveled to Mexico and visited seven national parks and countless state parks in California and throughout the American Southwest. Theo loved camping trips with family and friends. His final camping trip was at a beautiful lakeside campground in Glacier National Park in early July. At home, Theo was known in his family for his adorable clumsiness, his sense of humor, his love of funny TV shows, and his love of family pets Rocky and Barry. He loved music and created playlists to listen to on long car rides and at home. He was kind and empathetic, always making sure to include friends and make everyone feel welcome. His best friend was his younger brother Ray. Only 21 months apart, they were often mistaken for twins, and they spent every moment outside of school together. He filled every single day of his nine years of life with profound joy, love, and kindness. Theo will be missed by everyone who was lucky enough to know him. A small memorial was held for Theo is Los Angeles on September 11. Donations in his memory may be made to the Sierra Club or the SPCA. Theo Emerson
